articles.title: Future NBA Power Rankings for the Next 3 Years
articles.summary: The veteran-led New York Knicks are defending NBA champions, and they won their title by going through the rising San Antonio Spurs. Which of those two teams is most likely to reach the mountaintop over the next three seasons, and who else might join them in the climb?
articles.body:
The veteran-led New York Knicks are defending NBA champions, and they won their title by going through the rising San Antonio Spurs. Which of those two teams is most likely to reach the mountaintop over the next three seasons, and who else might join them in the climb?

To set up a multi-year power rankings like this, we first have to consider present strength, the best indicator of how good a team will be in the future. Hold onto the talent that's making you effective today, and the odds are pretty strong your high level will hold—unless injuries, trades or decline mess up the operation.

That last part is where the exercise gets interesting. We know some teams are on the downswing of their competitive arcs, and we also know that up-and-comers will overtake them.

Which up-and-comers? That's where the (informed) guesswork comes in. We need to evaluate which younger teams will rise as some of the older and less stable ones fall.

We have to look at where each team is now, what its trajectory might lead to in the near future and what tools it has to affect that rise or fall. We might even need to think about which way a team might steer itself. Bottoming out on purpose is still an option.

We have a three-year window, beginning in 2026-27, to rank the organizations most likely to succeed.

History impacts the Sacramento Kings' future more than it does that of any other team.

The organization has cycled through countless coaches, executives, lottery picks, signings and trade acquisitions over the years, producing exactly one postseason appearance since 2006. Vivek Ranadivé has been Sacramento's principal owner for the last 13 years of that stretch.

He is the constant in all that mismanagement and failure, and he's still making decisions. In fact, one of the Kings' many recent blunders, taking back Zach LaVine after botching their relationship with and trading De'Aaron Fox, came at a time when Ranadivé had " taken control of personnel power ."

The Kings are in far better shape than teams like the Phoenix Suns in the draft-asset category. The only one of their future firsts they don't control is in 2031. LaVine's contract will expire after this season. Darius Acuff Jr., Sacramento's most recent lottery pick, might turn into something.

But this team is in the cellar now, has no clearly projectable stars and, most importantly, is still run by an owner who has produced the least success in the entire league while in charge.

Even if Derik Queen pops, Jeremiah Fears builds on his rookie season and Zion Williamson stays relatively healthy, it'll be hard to see the New Orleans Pelicans as more than a Play-In threat between now and 2029.

That means the wisest course involves trading Trey Murphy III for two or three first-rounders and retooling for a post-Zion run at relevance. Of course, that's been the pretty obvious move for a while now, and the Pels haven't shown an inclination to make it.

New Orleans controls all of its own future first-round picks from 2028 to 2033, and next season's will be the most favorable of its own and Milwaukee's. The runway is clear for a more thorough rebuild a couple of years from now, but Williamson and the large contracts belonging to Dejounte Murray and Jordan Poole clog up the books at the moment.

Lastly, nothing the management combo of Joe Dumars and Troy Weaver has done since taking over inspires confidence. All things being equal, we should expect less from New Orleans than most teams with its assets and roster.

The Brooklyn Nets' roster might be the least threatening in the league, though that could change if they use Michael Porter Jr.'s expiring salary to bring back a player who could take on a first-option role beyond this season. The other top talents, led by second-year guard Egor Dëmin and rookie Mikel Brown Jr., are a long way from stardom.

Jordi Fernandez is a good coach who gets whatever talent he has to play hard, and the Nets don't have a bad contract on the books. They've had Fernandez and flexibility before, though, and the losses keep piling up.

A great candidate to finish in the relegation zone this season, Brooklyn is a draft or two and a big free-agent haul away from relevance.

Updated Rankings After Kuminga Signing 📊

Offseason Overreactions for Every Team 🫨

Devin Booker is a very good player, but not one worthy of the four years and $250 million remaining on his current contract.

It'll be awfully tough for the Suns to bring in somebody as good or better than Booker while paying Bradley Beal $19.4 million every year through 2029-30 not to play for them.

Phoenix is also bereft of draft capital, having most recently dealt away its unprotected 2033 first-rounder to bring Miles Bridges aboard from Charlotte. That's the kind of move a surefire contender makes to add the final piece of the puzzle, not one you'd expect from a squad that shocked the world by winning just 45 games a year ago.

The Suns may not be able to deal Booker for positive value because of his contract. They have the league's smallest stockpile of draft capital and are fairly committed to a roster that might top out as a Play-In team over the next three seasons. The only good news is that this exercise covers only a three-year timeline, and Phoenix could be moderately competitive this coming season.

If we expanded the exercise to look further into the future, Phoenix's outlook would be even bleaker.

All those years of trading draft capital and taking on expensive deals to appease Giannis Antetokounmpo leave the Milwaukee Bucks in whatever developmental stage comes before a rebuild.

Milwaukee is on the hook for $21.3 million in waived-and-stretched salary for Damian Lillard annually through 2029-30. It doesn't control its own first-round pick until 2031, and the two incoming firsts it received from Miami won't arrive until the next decade.

Lacking a cornerstone and very likely to flip most of the roster within the next couple of years, the Bucks are paying the price for hanging onto Antetokounmpo a little too long. It's hard to fault them; giving up on the best player in modern franchise history isn't easy.

Rookie Brayden Burries shone in Summer League, and Milwaukee should be able to get positive value for Myles Turner, Tyler Herro, and a few others in trades. The Bucks took the first, hardest step in starting over. But they have many more to make before they're a threat to do any consistent winning.

A year ago, the Memphis Grizzlies dealt away Desmond Bane to trigger a teardown that would eventually send Jaren Jackson Jr. and Ja Morant out the door after him. It's hard to believe how promising they look in the wake of a total overhaul like that.

No, the Grizzlies don't figure to be playoff threats any time soon. But rookie Cam Boozer might be their best player by November, and a hoard of incoming picks from the Bane and Jackson trades means a win-now trade will be possible as soon as the option presents itself. Memphis could have as many as six extra first-rounders coming in from other teams between now and 2031.

We need to be careful in overvaluing flexibility and youth, two qualities the Grizzlies have in abundance. The trick is turning those things into a product that can win games on the floor. For all of Memphis' long-term potential, it's difficult to imagine a consistent winner emerging until at least 2028.

After years of hanging around the league's "meh" middle, refusing to fully rebuild and showing little ambition to spend what it takes to contend, the Chicago Bulls finally seem to have picked a direction. They're getting younger, starting fresh and under the new management of Executive Vice President Bryson Graham.

Chicago isn't necessarily going to tank because the payoff is less certain in the new lottery environment, but it does seem more likely to trust its youth and avoid chasing the Zach LaVines and DeMar DeRozans of the world over the next three years. That's to say the Bulls are building deliberately, rather than hunting quick fixes.

Caleb Wilson is bursting with potential, and Matas Buzelis could be a quality starter on both ends as soon as this season. Maybe Norman Powell's $21.5 million salary will return a first-rounder at the February deadline.

Things aren't as aimless and bleak in Chicago as they once were, but this season feels like the early phase of a process that won't be complete until after our three-year timeline is over.

Let's assume the Kawhi Leonard trade goes through and the LA Clippers avoid meaningful league penalties following an ESPN report that the NBA found no evidence owner Steve Ballmer circumvented the salary cap in connection with Leonard.

In that hypothetical, the Clippers have a core of Darius Garland and Brandon Ingram with Keaton Wagler, Jordan Miller and Yanic Konan Niederhäuser providing youthful upside.

Optimistically, L.A.'s capable veteran role players—Rui Hachimura, Derrick Jones Jr., Brook Lopez, Kris Dunn—could contribute to a group that hangs around .500 and challenges for a Play-In spot for a couple of years.

The draft won't offer much help, as the Clippers don't have a first-rounder until 2030—assuming the league doesn't dock them one or two.

The market in Los Angeles and a deep-pocketed owner willing to spend aggressively to compete are both helpful factors. The Clippers have shown a willingness to swing big deals in the past and should be expected to do so again.

The baseline they're starting from just isn't all that high, though, and the Clippers also don't have the draft assets to pull off something like what they did in getting Paul George and Leonard in 2019.

If Kyrie Irving returns at close to top form, Dereck Lively II finally stays healthy enough to build on the stellar rookie season he enjoyed in 2023-24 and Cooper Flagg fast-tracks himself into the All-NBA conversation, the Dallas Mavericks could make some serious noise as soon as this year.

That scenario requires a clean sweep of good breaks and probably isn't the likeliest outcome. The safe bet is on the Mavericks being at least a couple of years away from real relevance, and by that time Irving may have aged out.

He, at least, could bring back a good trade return if he's moderately healthy. A deal like that would suggest the Mavs are retrenching, though, which would make it tough for them to profile as a playoff team until they acquire another rising star to pair with Flagg.

That player probably won't be arriving in the draft. Dallas doesn't have outright control over its first-round pick until 2031.

The Golden State Warriors aren't as good as many fans would like them to be right now, as Stephen Curry enters the final few seasons of his career. Nobody is in love with the team returning a 37-45 roster for 2026-27.

The good news is that their repeated refusal to send off massive asset packages for a Curry-supporting star means the Dubs also won't be as bad as some expect when Steph is gone.

Golden State has full control of all but one of its first-round picks through 2033, currently has no bad money on the books beyond this season and could use Jimmy Butler's $56.8 million expiring salary to reel in more picks or a star on a longer deal this season.

Much depends on the size of Curry's looming extension. If he takes the full max, it'll make it much harder for the Dubs to give him a contending roster. A team-friendlier deal could create some intriguing possibilities if the Dubs also get serious about adding high-end talent and putting all those picks on the table.

Ends of eras, which the Warriors are approaching, can be difficult. But Golden State is actually better prepared than most to stay relevant if and when Curry is gone toward the end of this three-year window.

The Washington Wizards' official timeline is "all of them."

How else to describe a squad that probably needs to win right now while Anthony Davis is still in the last stages of his prime (if healthy), while also committing to a late-20s Trae Young and rostering the most recent No. 1 overall pick in AJ Dybantsa?

Those are the Wizards' three most expensive players this coming season, though the overall roster will get costlier when extensions for Alex Sarr, Bilal Coulibaly, Kyshawn George and Tre Johnson enter the picture.

If Davis isn't traded and Young plays his best ball, the Wizards could thread the needle here by performing like a playoff team in the short term while Dybantsa and the other youngsters develop. Maybe in a year or two, Washington's recently drafted core will be ready to either play at the level of AD and Trae or take over from them as they age out.

There's real potential here, even if the plan seems disjointed, and the Wizards control all their own future firsts. They can add to...whatever this is...if they want to.

Ja Morant is currently slated to be the Portland Trail Blazers' highest-paid player in each of the next two seasons. Our projections have to consider the possibility that the former star's salary is effectively a dead cap hit, even while acknowledging there's a non-zero chance Morant is actually worth that money.

Even if Morant hits the higher end of his possible outcomes, the Blazers' roster is oddly constructed with a glut of guards and not enough shooting to make sense around Deni Avdija. Having now seen Avdija prove over a season-and-a-half that he can dominate games as a driver, you'd think the Blazers would have made opening up the floor with better spacing a priority.

There's enough upside-laden talent here between Avdija, Donovan Clingan, Scoot Henderson and Shaedon Sharpe to retain optimism about a leap. Temper that with the knowledge that owner Tom Dundon is an epic cheapskate who might extend his thriftiness to player payroll while alienating fans with his threats to move the team.

Based on the money they're paying over the next three years, the Orlando Magic have already chosen their core. They'll spend $154 million on Paolo Banchero, Franz Wagner, Jalen Suggs and Desmond Bane next year, and that number will only go up through 2028-29.

Toss in an average salary of $19 million per year for Wendell Carter Jr. during that same stretch, and Orlando is basically at (and later over) the salary cap between just five players. That's without factoring in Anthony Black's looming extension.

Banchero is the key figure. He needs to prove he can knock down threes and ditch his ball-stopping ways to make good on his No. 1 pick pedigree and max extension. Just 24, he should have plenty of growth ahead. Note, though, that Orlando has already changed coaches by replacing Jamahl Mosley with Sean Sweeney. If the Magic's offense doesn't take a step forward, a Banchero trade could be the next move.

While the Magic could get positive value for Banchero and basically every other highly-paid player on the roster, that kind of deal might only bring back picks and set the organization back a year or two.

There's real upside here, but the Magic could be closer to a soft rebuild than it seems.

Some view the LaMelo Ball trade as an intentional step backward, but the presences of Kon Knueppel and Brandon Miller mean the Charlotte Hornets still have the potential stars they need to climb the standings between now and 2029.

While Ball clearly made those two better when sharing the floor last year, Knueppel and Miller could both expand their games in larger roles. Charlotte could use the flexibility and draft capital it gained in the Ball trade to fill in around its new core, and we should give this organization the benefit of the doubt.

The Hornets have won virtually every transaction they've made in recent seasons, highlighted by a series of moves that resulted in sending the Suns back their own 2029 first-rounder for an unprotected 2033 pick. That selection won't feature in Charlotte's three-year window (unless it goes out in a trade), but it exemplifies the smart, measured thinking that has the Hornets so well positioned.

You don't trade an entire rotation and every draft pick that's not nailed down for a 31-year-old two-time MVP if you're focused on the distant future.

The Miami Heat's acquisition of Giannis Antetokounmpo was solely motivated by a desire to win right now. Whether they can put together a good enough supporting cast to maximize their title chances around Giannis and Bam Adebayo remains to be seen, though the 2026-27 version of the squad looks like it'll have some serious depth issues.

You have to squint hard to imagine the Heat belonging among the East's top threats this coming season. While that could change if Antetokounmpo's presence attracts free-agent interest over the next couple of summers, we also need to consider Antetokounmpo's health issues last year and what they might mean for his performance level going forward.

It's very possible we're past the days of relying on Giannis as a top-five superstar, which means Miami's desperation for depth will only intensify as he ages.

The San Antonio Spurs control the Atlanta Hawks' first-round picks in 2027 and 2028, which actually makes success over the next three years more likely. The option to bottom out, devalued by lottery reform, is not on the table.

The Hawks wouldn't pursue that path anyway. They have too much young talent, led by 24-year-old All-NBA third-teamer Jalen Johnson, to consider tanking.

Johnson's $30 million salary through 2029-30 assures he'll remain one of the most underpaid stars in the league, giving Atlanta flexibility other teams should envy. Onyeka Okongwu and Nickeil Alexander-Walker give the Hawks two more underpaid quality starters, both still in their 20s.

Atlanta's real upside lies in its ready-made setup for a star better than Johnson. The payroll is under control with no large long-term commitments, the roster is loaded with movable salaries and role players who'd benefit from moving down a spot in the pecking order, and the Hawks still have plenty of their own picks and a juicy one coming in from either Milwaukee or New Orleans in 2027.

The Hawks are ripe for a major acquisition that could put them in the fringe-contender class at some point over the next three years.

Until the Kawhi Leonard trade resolves, it's hard to determine where the Toronto Raptors belong in a set of power rankings.

If we assume the trade with the Clippers goes through as expected, Toronto probably deserves to be considered a second-tier contender that could at least reach the 2027 Conference Finals.

That presumes good health and that Leonard holds up in his age-35 season. The longer-term outlook is a little less enticing than the one for next year, but even if Leonard slips a little, it's hard to argue the Raptors' three-year run with him will be any less successful than it would have been with Brandon Ingram and Gradey Dick.

Scottie Barnes offers stability and a high floor as a 25-year-old All-NBA stud who showed last postseason that he could run a credible offense while bringing elite defensive impact. He and Collin Murray-Boyles should ensure Toronto defends better than most through 2029.

Leonard is the swing piece. We'll just slot the Raptors here, based as much on Barnes' ascent as the hope that Kawhi shows up and stays healthy for a year or two.

The Utah Jazz should be in contention for a playoff spot this season, a welcome change after several years of deliberate losing. All that purposeful failure yielded Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey, two core pieces who could develop into positive starters toward the end of our three-year window.

Bailey showed enough promise to project as a helpful rotation player who could start in 2026-27, and he'll join a handful of stars—Keyonte George, Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr.—to give the Jazz the right mix of experience and upside.

None of the three first-round picks Utah sent to Memphis for Jackson were its own, so flexibility is still a factor here. If the Jazz want to add to their core, they have the assets and matching salary to acquire a superstar.

Though not a likely contender given the current roster, the combination of in-prime stars, youthful upside and movable draft capital makes the Jazz an intriguing bet to reach that level by 2029.

As long as they don't overcommit on Amen Thompson's rookie-scale extension, the Houston Rockets can easily trade all of their best players for positive value.

A bevy of deals that flips over the roster isn't Plan A, but the ability to pivot easily if the need arises helps their outlook.

Ideally, Houston will get continued development from Alperen Sengün (24), Reed Sheppard (22) and Thompson (23) while vets Kevin Durant, Steven Adams and Fred VanVleet all hang onto their current production levels.

Half-court offense seems like it'll be a problem for as long as Sengün and Thompson are key pieces of the puzzle, but a breakthrough could be possible if one or the other makes a leap as a shooter.

The Rockets are about as dangerous as a team can be without a clear "best on a title-winner" player. Sengün has made back-to-back All-Star games and probably comes closest, but he needs to take another step or two before Houston will have the necessary top option to tangle with Wembanyama and SGA out west.

Nikola Jokić could be gone in free agency as soon as the summer of 2027, Jamal Murray's deal may be too large to trade for positive value if things go south and the Nuggets have dealt away so many future firsts that they're now stuck with only three swaps to trade.

The bottom could fall out very quickly in Denver, and recovery would be a long and painful process. At the moment, Christian Braun is the only Nuggets player on a fully guaranteed salary for 2029-30.

Really, this comes down to Jokić. We're taking him at his word that he intends to play out his career in Denver, and we're assuming his skill and processing speed will keep him in the MVP conversation as he ages into his 30s over the next three years. But if he walks, the Nuggets will immediately find themselves in one of the bleakest situations anywhere in the league.

One potential third option, trading Jokić ahead of his upcoming free agency, would replenish Denver's assets and avoid a worst-case scenario. It's hard to imagine the organization dealing the best player in franchise history, but we shouldn't rule it out if Jokić communicates an intent to leave.

Anthony Edwards, LaMelo Ball and Jaden McDaniels are all under contract through 2028-29, which means the Minnesota Timberwolves have most of the key ingredients they'll need to stick among the West's top playoff threats for the foreseeable future.

Rudy Gobert is 34 but has held up well enough during his time with the Wolves to raise the possibility he'll remain an All-Defense force for a few more years. As long as his decline is gentle (and as long as he takes a pay cut on his next deal), the Wolves will be dangerous on both ends.

This team's ceiling depends on the synergy between Ball and Edwards. Brought aboard to lighten the playmaking load on Edwards, Ball has to prove he's kicked the injury bug. He must also defend with respectable effort and mature off the floor. If this goes well and Edwards benefits from Ball's control of the offense, something special could develop.

Charlotte gave up on LaMelo for a reason, though, and we can't ignore the downside risk Minnesota took on by adding him. Short on draft capital, very expensive and at least peripherally aware of 29 other teams hoping Edwards gets a wandering eye, the Wolves' position is more precarious than it might seem.

Luka Dončić is under contract through 2027-28 with a player option for 2028-29, which means he'll be around for at least two of the three years we're considering.

That is, unless he tires of ownership turnover, decides he'd actually like to choose where he plays for the first time in his career or otherwise determines Los Angeles isn't for him.

None of that seems especially likely at the moment, and the Lakers have bent over backwards to build the supporting cast Dončić wants, including Walker Kessler.

Even with Dončić, Austin Reaves and Kessler, it's hard to view the Lakers in the same contender class occupied by the Spurs, Thunder, Knicks and others. Given the assets Los Angeles sent out to get Kessler, its resources to improve the roster are limited.

In other words, the Lakers' ability to move up these rankings depends mostly on Dončić staying healthy, happy and perhaps even finding a new level as he moves closer to 30. None of those are sure things.

The Indiana Pacers are pretty committed to their current core, which is both encouraging and concerning.

Indy was a win from a championship in 2025 and could be even better this year with Ivica Zubac joining a recovered Tyrese Haliburton and a gracefully aging Pascal Siakam. Aaron Nesmith, Andrew Nembhard, Obi Toppin and T.J. McConnell are all still around from that Eastern Conference champion squad, and offseason addition Kelly Oubre Jr. deepens the rotation.

If the Pacers get anything from Jarace Walker, Ben Sheppard or Johnny Furphy, they'll supplement the entrenched vets with some younger options.

That's the encouraging part. The worry arises when considering the uncertainty of Zubac's fit, Haliburton's potentially bumpy recovery and Siakam's possible slippage as he begins his age-32 season in 2026-27.

The only first-rounder the Pacers don't control is their 2031 selection, so they can tinker with trades if they need to. Ultimately, though, this team's window depends on Haliburton and Co. proving they're the contenders they once were.

Few teams have a higher three-year variance than the Philadelphia 76ers, whose ceiling depends on Joel Embiid staying healthy and LeBron James continuing to buck the aging trend as he gets deeper into his 40s.

You've got to acknowledge Philly's potential this season with the addition of James and Jaylen Brown, even if Embiid is not a good bet to play more than half the year or be in good form when the playoffs roll around. Brown, James and Tyrese Maxey will keep the Sixers highly relevant, but it'll probably take a miraculous turning back of the clock from Embiid to reach contender status.

The downside in Philadelphia is deeply concerning.

Embiid is probably the worst contract in the league at the moment, and it could actually get worse if his health and mobility continue to decline. The Celtics gave up on Brown partly because they don't believe he's worth what he's making. James' run has to end at some point.

Between Maxey and VJ Edgecombe, the Sixers have pieces that can lead them into their next era. But they're the only stable part of an otherwise very shaky (though intriguing) short-term build.

Though it sounds strange to say about a 60-win team led by a legitimate 24-year-old MVP candidate in Cade Cunningham, the Detroit Pistons are at a crossroads.

The way they resolve Jalen Duren's restricted free agency and the looming extension decision for Ausar Thompson will either leave them with the flexibility to pivot in their roster construction around Cunningham or lock them into a flawed (while promising) core.

Duren has already earned an All-NBA nod, and last postseason's no-show effort probably won't repeat itself. The Pistons are right to play hardball with him in restricted free agency, and they should be able to retain him on a contract that doesn't preclude the addition of another star or better playmaking depth down the line.

Thompson is a trickier proposition. He's a top-one-percent athlete with exceptionally disruptive talent on D, but he's an underwhelming playmaker who can't shoot a lick. Detroit will box itself in if it pays him like a future star—unless he makes dramatic improvements on offense.

The Pistons are going to contend for top-four position in the East as long as Cunningham is healthy and the defense holds up. Whether they can do more than that depends on keeping their books under control.

If Jayson Tatum regains his full form, the Boston Celtics should have the down-ballot MVP candidate they need to build a contending roster. Paired with a head coach in Joe Mazzulla and a tactical scheme that emphasizes winning the shot-math game, the Celtics have also proved that they can get more out of their roster than most.

The Jaylen Brown trade will have a major effect on the next three years in one of two ways. It'll either be remembered as the bold move that freed up cash and restocked the draft cupboard while unloading an overrated player, or the deal that officially knocked the Celtics out of serious contention during the Tatum era.

Right now, it's hard to argue next year's version of the team will be better without Brown. But we need to trust Brad Stevens and a management group that has gotten a lot of its decisions right over the years. Hugo Gonzalez, Baylor Scheierman, Jordan Walsh, Neemias Queta and others are proof Boston can draft, acquire and develop talent with limited resources.

As long as they don't trade 25-year-old Evan Mobley, the Cleveland Cavaliers should have a high defensive floor. Donovan Mitchell's recent re-commitment to the team on an extension that keeps him locked up through 2029-30 also assures the presence of a lead offensive option with multiple All-NBA nods.

Peyton Watson fits right between those two stars and could be the reason Cleveland ditches the not-quite-contender status it has held for the last handful of seasons.

The Cavs have been extremely expensive for a while, and Mobley's extension will take up 30 percent of the cap for most of the next half-decade. Without control of a first-rounder until 2030, Cleveland is also short on flexibility. If things go very wrong, a reset that involves a Mitchell and/or Mobley trade could restock the cupboards.

For now, the Cavs feel like a lock to win 55-plus games and should scare teams more than ever with Watson's defense and athleticism joining the operation.

The defending champion New York Knicks should stick in the contender class for at least another year or two, but there's no denying they lack the shelf life of some other teams ahead of them in the rankings.

Jalen Brunson's craft, post game and willpower should age well, but are we sure Karl-Anthony Towns has another couple of postseason runs in him as good as the one he completed in June? And wasn't Mikal Bridges' waxing and waning impact a story throughout both the regular season and playoffs?

Those three and Josh Hart will play the upcoming season on the wrong side of 30, and OG Anunoby is 29. Steep decline isn't imminent, but the Knicks certainly aren't expecting any of their core rotation pieces from the title run to improve as the years advance.

The Knicks' championship run means they deserve our full respect, but we need to be realistic about where they are on the aging curve relative to some of the competition near them in the rankings.

An in-prime MVP, two All-NBA stars locked into long-term deals that'll never pay them more than 25 percent of the cap and a deep supporting cast built by a front office that knows what it's doing—the Oklahoma City Thunder have it all.

Well, except for the upper hand in their most recent postseason meeting with the San Antonio Spurs.

Jalen Williams' hamstring injury had plenty to do with OKC falling in the Western Conference Finals, but Williams and Chet Holmgren have lengthy enough injury histories to warrant real concern about their durability going forward.

And while two-time reigning MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is probably the best player in the league right now, Victor Wembanyama could seize that title early next season and hold onto it for a decade.

Oklahoma City has won at least 60 games for two years running, and none of its main weapons is in the decline phase yet. The Thunder can hold this level for at least another three seasons. San Antonio, though, feels like it has only just begun its rise.

Health is the biggest obstacle between the San Antonio Spurs and at least one championship between now and 2029. They already checked the "learn a hard lesson" box by losing to the Knicks in the Finals, when inexperience in key moments proved costly.

With that out of the way, Victor Wembanyama, Dylan Harper and Stephon Castle should complete the team's ultimate objective sooner than later.

The Spurs will likely begin 2026-27 as title favorites, and Wembanyama should be the preseason MVP pick. Harper is a superstar in waiting, and he joined Castle in proving himself ready to compete at the absolute highest level. Wemby is the oldest of the three at just 23.

With plenty of draft capital to swing a trade for another star, the Spurs may not be done adding to the roster. If they can figure out how to turn De'Aaron Fox's salary slot into a more useful player to balance out the rotation, the gap between them and the Thunder could widen.

Stats courtesy of NBA.com , Basketball Reference and Cleaning the Glass . Salary info via Spotrac .

Grant Hughes covers the NBA for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, where he appears with Bleacher Report's Dan Favale .

articles.title: How Jaylen Brown Trade Talks Unfolded with Celtics' Brad Stevens Revealed by 76ers' Bob Myers
articles.summary: Philadelphia 76ers executive Bob Myers provided some insight this week into how the organization's acquisition of Jaylen Brown from the Boston Celtics came to be this offseason.
articles.body:
Philadelphia 76ers executive Bob Myers provided some insight this week into how the organization's acquisition of Jaylen Brown from the Boston Celtics came to be this offseason.

During an appearance on Cousins with Vince Carter & Tracy McGrady (h/t HoopsHype.com ), Myers discussed coming to the realization that Brown was actually available and negotiating with Celtics president of basketball operations Brad Stevens (beginning at the 23:50 mark of the podcast) :

Michael Jordan expected to leave media role

Updated Rankings After Kuminga Signing 📊

"You start hearing there was a possibility, and the job then became is this a real thing with Jaylen Brown? Is it a real thing," Myers said. "I think Brad Stevens is one of the most straight shooters in the league. So when you work in the NBA as an executive, you ultimately, usually have at least one or two—I don't want to say transactions—with every other GM. So you know, if I call Tracy, I go, 'Hey, you want to make a deal?' He might be like, yeah, yeah, yeah, and then he doesn't. ...

"But you have to understand, like, he's honest, or he might tell me what I want to hear, or he might lie to me. This dude just might just lie. He lied to me two years ago, he's going to lie to me again. That's not Brad Stevens. So when Brad Stevens responded with, 'What are you offering,' then you knew that there was a shot."

Brown's name came up in trade rumors throughout the offseason, but they were usually linked to the Celtics' pursuit of Giannis Antetokounmpo.

Once the Milwaukee Bucks decided to trade Giannis to the Miami Heat, though, the rumors and speculation surrounding Brown didn't go away.

Ultimately, Boston agreed to send Brown to Philly in exchange for Paul George, two first-round picks and two second-round picks in the biggest blockbuster trade of the offseason.

The Sixers acquired a five-time All-Star, one-time NBA champion and one-time NBA Finals MVP in Brown, who was also coming off the best statistical season of his career.

As Boston's No. 1 scoring option for most of the 2025-26 campaign, Brown averaged a career-high 28.7 points, 6.9 rebounds and 5.1 assists per game.

In addition to adding Brown to a core that already included Tyrese Maxey, Joel Embiid and VJ Edgecombe, the acquisition of Brown also seemingly played a huge role in convincing LeBron James to sign with the team in free agency.

Now, the 76ers have arguably the best starting five in the NBA, and one of their best chances to win a championship since they last did so in 1983.

Boston Celtics president of basketball operations Brad Stevens expressed his belief this week that Jaylen Brown's No. 7 jersey will one day be retired by the organization.

According to Avery Hill of the Boston Globe , Stevens brought up the topic during a discussion about the difficulties of being a front-office decision-maker in the NBA.

"I get a lot of emails and a lot of people that ask about wanting to be a GM," Stevens said. "I'm like, 'I wish you would've been around last summer when we basically had to trade Jrue Holiday.' That's like brutal. Or we go through this long arduous process and ultimately decide to trade Jaylen, whose numbers will likely go up in the rafters in Boston. Not fun."

Both Brown and Holiday were crucial parts of the Celtics' championship team in 2024 with Brown being named NBA Finals MVP.

Despite that accolade, along with his five All-Star selections in 10 seasons with the Celtics, Brown was traded to the Philadelphia 76ers this offseason for Paul George and draft picks, ending his hugely successful run in Boston.

articles.title: Luka Doncic's Lakers Future Addressed by NBA Insider After Question About Potential Split
articles.summary: ESPN NBA insider Dave McMenamin expressed doubt Thursday regarding the possibility of Luka Dončić wanting to split with the Los Angeles Lakers any time soon.
articles.body:
ESPN NBA insider Dave McMenamin expressed doubt Thursday regarding the possibility of Luka Dončić wanting to split with the Los Angeles Lakers any time soon.

Discussing whether the 2026-27 season could be Dončić's last one with the Lakers, McMenamin suggested that nothing points to that being the case.

"Even with the Lakers' ownership about to change hands from Mark Walter to Josh Kushner and Bob Iger, it's hard to imagine the organization suddenly changing directions and not continuing to build with Dončić as the center of its universe," McMenamin wrote.

Michael Jordan expected to leave media role

Updated Rankings After Kuminga Signing 📊

"It's similarly unfathomable to believe that Dončić, who just footed a six-figure bill to host all of his teammates for a minicamp and camaraderie-growing retreat in Slovenia, would suddenly decide that he is done with the Lakers next summer."

Dončić signed a three-year, $160.34 million contract extension, including a player option for 2028-29, with the Lakers in August 2025.

While that extension was signed under the ownership of Walter, who agreed to sell the Lakers to Kushner and Iger two weeks ago, all signs point toward the Lakers continuing to build around Dončić.

Even with LeBron James in the fold last season, Dončić was clearly the go-to guy, as he averaged a league-leading 33.5 points per game to go along with 8.3 assists and 7.7 rebounds en route to a fourth-place finish in the NBA MVP voting.

James subsequently left the Lakers and signed with the Philadelphia 76ers this offseason, erasing any doubt about who the Lakers' on-court leader is.

Perhaps things could change if the Lakers struggle this coming season or if Dončić clashes with the new ownership group, but as of now, he is clearly the Lakers' foundation and their best chance at contending in the coming years.

articles.title: Anthony Davis, Kyrie Irving Trades Eyed by NBA Insiders in New Poll Ahead of 2026-27 Season
articles.summary: Having already popped up in trade rumors this offseason, Anthony Davis and Kyrie Irving remain popular candidates to get moved at some point during the 2026-27 NBA season.
articles.body:
Having already popped up in trade rumors this offseason, Anthony Davis and Kyrie Irving remain popular candidates to get moved at some point during the 2026-27 NBA season.

In a survey of ESPN insiders who were asked about the next player to request a trade, Davis topped the poll with 10 points and Irving was second with four points.

Davis being so far out in front of everyone else comes in the wake of a report that the 10-time All-Star and Washington Wizards were putting off "any meaningful talks" about a contract extension until after the regular season begins.

Michael Jordan expected to leave media role

Updated Rankings After Kuminga Signing 📊

One of the primary reasons the Wizards might want to hold off on signing Davis is financially-motivated. ESPN's Tim MacMahon wrote as part of the survey that Davis and his agent, Rich Paul, "haven't been coy about their desire for a maximum (or close to it) contract extension."

Irving's future with the Dallas Mavericks has been a topic of conversation dating back to last season. He was seen as a potential candidate to be moved prior to the trade deadline in February, but the Mavs were intrigued at the time about the possibility of seeing him in a lineup with Cooper Flagg.

Dallas' outlook has changed significantly since then with the hiring of Masai Ujiri as team president and giving him full authority to do what he wants to reshape the roster moving forward.

There are practical reasons for the Mavs and Wizards to be patient in exploring trade opportunities for the star players. Irving hasn't played since tearing his ACL in March 2025, sitting out the entire 2025-26 season while rehabbing the injury.

Washington hasn't seen Davis in a game since acquiring him from the Mavs in February. He appeared in a total of 29 games with Dallas after being part of the Luka Dončić trade in February 2025.

One potentially significant complicating factor for teams interested in Davis or Irving is their respective contracts. Both players are entering the final guaranteed season on their current deals, but they have player options for 2027-28.

Davis' option is worth $62.8 million . Irving's is slightly more team-friendly at $42.4 million .

The max deal for Davis is four years and $273 million . A healthy Davis and Trae Young around 2026 No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa, Bub Carrington, Alex Sarr and Bilal Coulibaly makes the Wizards an intriguing team to watch, but the availability of those top two players will determine their ceiling next season.

Dallas largely knows what it has with Flagg, even if he has just started to scratch the surface of his potential. The development of Morez Johnson Jr., the ninth pick in the 2026 draft, and health of Dereck Lively II are keys for the Mavs to reach their full potential next season.

Irving, who will turn 35 during the season, doesn't seem like a long-term solution for the Mavericks given where they are in their roster build around Flagg.

articles.title: Kyle Lowry's No. 7 Jersey to Be Retired by Raptors During Game vs. LeBron James, 76ers
articles.summary: After officially retiring as a member of the Toronto Raptors earlier this summer, the franchise will honor Kyle Lowry by retiring his jersey number during the 2026-27 NBA season.
articles.body:
After officially retiring as a member of the Toronto Raptors earlier this summer, the franchise will honor Kyle Lowry by retiring his jersey number during the 2026-27 NBA season.

The Raptors announced on Thursday they will hang Lowry's No. 7 jersey from the rafters at Scotiabank Arena during a ceremony after their Jan. 10 game against the Philadelphia 76ers.

Lowry ended his storied 20-year NBA career on July 7 by signing a one-day contract with the Raptors to formally retire with the club he played for from 2012 to '21.

The Raptors choosing their game against the Sixers to retire Lowry's jersey is fitting since Philadelphia was the team he spent the final two years of his career with. He is also from Philadelphia and played college basketball at Villanova.

Lowry made one of his final appearances for the 76ers against the Raptors in Toronto. He played the final two minutes of Philadelphia's 115-102 win on Jan. 12 after Raptors fans chanted for him to get in the game.

The Raptors originally acquired Lowry in a trade with the Houston Rockets in July 2012. He was instrumental in turning the franchise into a perennial playoff contender and eventually winning an NBA title during the 2018-19 season.

Lowry made six All-Star appearances in nine seasons with Toronto. He ranks top two in franchise history in games played (601), minutes played (20,813) and total points scored (10,540), steals (873) and triple-doubles (16).

Vince Carter's No. 15 is the only other jersey the Raptors have retired among players who appeared in a game for the franchise. Bill Russell's No. 6 was retired league-wide in 2022.

articles.title: Ben Simmons' 'Fantastic' Kings Workout Detailed in New NBA Rumors amid Comeback Bid
articles.summary: The Sacramento Kings reportedly played host to a strong showing from free agent Ben Simmons after holding a private workout with the NBA veteran.
articles.body:
The Sacramento Kings reportedly played host to a strong showing from free agent Ben Simmons after holding a private workout with the NBA veteran.

Sactown Sports 1140's Carmichael Dave said Wednesday someone who viewed the workouts texted him that Simmons "looked fantastic."

Dave previously reported Kings general manager Scott Perry went to Florida to watch Simmons work out.

Simmons, who turned 30 in July, last played in the NBA during a 2024-25 campaign he split between the Brooklyn Nets and Los Angeles Clippers.

The Philadelphia 76ers' top pick in the 2016 draft, Simmons dealt with back injuries that derailed the last few seasons of his NBA career.

He played 51 games in his last NBA season, but told Clay Skipper of Men's Health earlier this offseason he had been playing through pain due to a nerve injury.

Simmons also told Skipper he was feeling great and planning to make a return to the NBA.

The Kings have two roster spots remaining. The franchise could fill up both with minimum contracts without exceeding the luxury tax, per CapSheets' Yossi Gozlan .

ESPN's Marc J. Spears reported earlier this month Simmons had "an offer from a West team to come to training camp."

NBA insider Jake Fischer reported the following week the Kings had started a series of workouts featuring veteran players.

Veterans the Kings had shown interest in include Cam Payne, Victor Oladipo and Elfrid Payton, according to Fischer.

Payne played 22 games last season for the Philadelphia 76ers as a fringe rotation player who missed time due to a hamstring injury.

Oladipo and Payton, like Simmons, are both looking to make a return to the NBA after time away from the league.

Payton last played in 2024-25 for the New Orleans Pelicans and Charlotte Hornets, while Oladipo hasn't seen NBA action since the 2022-23 campaign.

Simmons' health and the status of these other NBA veterans could impact which direction the Kings ultimately take as the franchise looks to add depth before rosters are finalized Oct. 19.

articles.title: Kevin Durant Reacts to Viral Photo 'Hiding' Behind Bush at Nobu in New Video Amid NBA Offseason
articles.summary: Houston Rockets star Kevin Durant says he wasn't attempting to hide in viral photos that seemingly showed him standing behind a bush outside the Malibu restaurant Nobu earlier this summer.
articles.body:
Houston Rockets star Kevin Durant says he wasn't attempting to hide in viral photos that seemingly showed him standing behind a bush outside the Malibu restaurant Nobu earlier this summer.

"You thought I was hiding behind a bush? This is insane," Durant told Speedy Morman in a Thursday appearance on Boardroom Talks . "Why would I hide behind a bush?"

Durant continued, "It made sense, it looked like I was, and then the headline was just crazy. But I don't need to hide, no. I was coming out Nobu, and it's like this tall grassy fence or whatever. I'm coming out just like everybody else."

Durant added that had he not wanted to be photographed he would not have chosen a restaurant he described as "the paparazzi capital."

The Daily Mail initially reported the photographs showed a moment in which 6-foot-11 Durant had "attempted to hide himself behind a tall bush."

Durant, who will turn 38 in September, is heading into his second season with the Houston Rockets after averaging 26 points per game last campaign.

He has spent parts of his offseason training with fellow All-Stars including Chet Holmgren and Paolo Banchero .

articles.title: Why Jonathan Kuminga choosing the Timberwolves feels like a win for both sides
articles.summary: The addition of Kuminga in Minnesota is a risk worth taking out West.
articles.body:
The previous installments of Timberwolves basketball, as menacing of a frontline it featured with the likes of Rudy Gobert , Karl-Anthony Towns , Julius Randle and Naz Reid , were all too predictable.

Minnesota 's modus operandi had always been to display its physicality on front street, a tour de force of brute strength designed to wear opponents down on both ends of the floor. The Wolves' aggressive approach, contextualized within the larger scope of the Western Conference and Anthony Edwards ' presence as a unicorn of sorts, defined their status as contenders over the last few seasons.

Their postseason elimination at the hands of the Spurs, however, forced a recalibration. Throughout the second-round series, San Antonio leaned on its speed, quickness and versatility to dismantle Minnesota at seemingly every turn. It certainly didn't help matters that Randle turned in one of his least-efficient offensive showings and Gobert was neutralized by his countryman, Victor Wembanyama , but it was clear something needed to change.

On Wednesday, free agent forward Jonathan Kuminga reportedly agreed to a two-year, $12.4 million deal to join the Wolves that includes a player option. It's the latest move in what has been a busy summer for president of basketball operations Tim Connelly and general manager Matt Lloyd, with star guard LaMelo Ball now in the fold and key reserve Ayo Dosunmu re-signed as well, and with both Randle and Reid traded to Brooklyn and Charlotte, respectively.

Let's put the financials aside for a moment. Yes, Kuminga's decision-making over the last few seasons, particularly as it relates to contractual wishes, has been iffy. The memes have been flying all over the internet (as well as the unfortunate comparisons to Dennis Schröder 's somewhat similar situation, turning down a substantial amount of money and never getting close to it again). But let's be honest here. From a flexibility standpoint — in late August — are we sure this is the choice to ridicule?

Perhaps Laker faithfuls feel strongly in the opposite direction given Kuminga's declining of a starting role there alongside Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves (although I truly believe that would have gone sour). At this stage of his career, he should be on prove-it deals, ensuring he can coexist on the most talented team he's ever been on without any hiccups. Six million dollars a year, with a chance to improve his stock before testing the free agency waters again in 2027 — if he so chooses to — feels like a win for both sides.

While there's a decent bet that Kuminga, who will turn 24 in October, may not be the "hand in glove" fit at power forward, there's enough surrounding talent to make the fit work. Recently, Connelly sat down with longtime reporter Jon Krawczynski and urged for a low-usage, high impact complementary player.

"We are going to have a lot of volume guys," Connelly said. "Jaden is going to have more volume. LaMelo and Ant are going to have a lot of volume. Ayo is going to have a huge volume. So what we need is guys who can do more with less … we're going to play a different brand of basketball."

Eschewing size for speed certainly comes with its tradeoffs, but Kuminga has shown how his intangibles (which often go unnoticed in a fast-paced NBA game) can pay dividends. Scaling down his usage will probably be a work in progress — high-volume types don't change course overnight — but other aspects of his game, particularly his rebounding prowess and versatility are worth gambling on, especially at that price point.

Outside of his rookie season, Kuminga has been one of the league's premier possession extenders and finishers at his position . Prior to his trade to Atlanta , the 23-year-old was rebounding at an extraordinary rate as an 88th percentile glass cleaner, leveraging his 6-foot-11 wingspan and athleticism to beat slower power forwards and centers on the boards. Randle was a lot of things in Minnesota, but a proficient rebounder was not one of them. Reid was at least decent in that aspect, but offered minimal impact on second-chance opportunities. For a team that will be learning on the fly with Ball and Edwards manning the controls, having a player like Kuminga who can offer more cracks in the half-court — for a team that finished 18th in both offensive and defensive rebounding rate — is important.

Earlier last season when Kuminga had actually earned a starting role with the Warriors, he was at his best serving as an off-ball threat, spacing the floor for other ball-handlers while offering his services as a slasher and cutter. He finished in the 80th percentile in points per possession off cuts, a skill that will definitely come in handy as defenses load up on the likes of Ball and Edwards. Kuminga is also excellent at drawing fouls , getting to the line on around 16% of his shots, and knows how to find pockets to attack, even with traditional bigs like Gobert on the floor. And in instances where one of Minnesota's superstars are off the floor, Kuminga has shown capable of serving as a secondary/tertiary operator, among the top third in assist rate for five straight seasons.

Defensively, there's no questioning whether Kuminga is an upgrade over Reid/Randle. His brief stint in Atlanta, surrounded by vastly more athletic talents than with the Warriors, offered a snapshot into what his impact can look like extrapolated to a larger scale. Per PBP Stats, the Hawks were a stunning +14 in Kuminga's minutes and held a defensive rating of 103.6. Now, we're not saying he's the best or most impactful defender in basketball — far from it — but he is smart, knows how to work within the constructs of a half-court scheme and can toggle between assignments in ways his predecessors simply could not. (Kuminga ranked in the 90th percentile in defensive versatility compared to 58th for Randle.)

Does this move come with questions? Of course. This is one of the more talented players who had to wait until nearly September to sort out his future. He hasn't been particularly effective in transition considering the opportunities he gets to run the floor, is an average outside shooter at best and his shot selection and overall decision-making has left his coaching staff scratching their heads at times. But the Wolves are gearing up for their biggest push yet and adding Kuminga, a low-cost, potentially high-impact move, is a risk worth taking out West.

articles.title: Kevin Durant Teases NBA Retirement Timeline in New Video After Russell Westbrook's Announcement
articles.summary: Kevin Durant watched former teammate Russell Westbrook retire this offseason and admitted the end of his own career might not be that far away.
articles.body:
Kevin Durant watched former teammate Russell Westbrook retire this offseason and admitted the end of his own career might not be that far away.

"I'm on deck," the future Hall of Famer said during an episode of Boardroom Talks (11:40 mark). "… It's a young man's game. Even though I still feel like I can play, I always hear, 'you're 38, you're 39. You're getting up there.' I get that. But I put everything into the game, and I'm cool with whatever happens moving forward. I'm going to continue putting everything into the game until I can't."

Durant entered the league as the No. 2 overall pick of a 2007 draft that still has a veteran presence in the league with Mike Conley and Al Horford. And while they are also near the end of their careers as well, Durant still occupies a different role.

After all, the 37-year-old was an All-NBA Second-Team selection last season as one of the best players in the league.

While he may not be quite as dominant as he was at his peak, the Texas product can still take over games and go back-and-forth with the NBA's elite. He averaged 26.0 points, 5.5 rebounds and 4.8 assists last season for the Houston Rockets while maintaining his incredible efficiency that has defined his tenure.

Durant shot 52 percent from the field and 41.3 percent from deep.

It isn't difficult to imagine him connecting on his smooth midrange jumpers and outside looks for the next five years at least, even if he loses some of his explosiveness when attacking the basket. He also answered some durability questions by appearing in 78 games in 2025-26, although he missed the majority of Houston's first-round loss to the Los Angeles Lakers.

When Durant does eventually retire, the NBA will be losing a legend.

His resume includes two championships, two NBA Finals MVPs, a league MVP, a Rookie of the Year, four scoring titles, 12 All-NBA selections, 16 All-Star nods and a spot on the NBA's 75th Anniversary Team.

Durant has helped define a generation in the league's history alongside players such as LeBron James and Stephen Curry, and is continuing to do so even if he is thinking about eventual retirement.

articles.title: Kevin Durant Reveals If He'd Take $100M Pay Cut to Chase NBA Title After Brunson, Knicks' Finals Run
articles.summary: New York Knicks point guard Jalen Brunson took $113 million less on his contract extension in 2024 to help give his team more financial flexibility to build a strong squad, and two years later, the Knicks won their first NBA championship in 53 seasons.
articles.body:
New York Knicks point guard Jalen Brunson took $113 million less on his contract extension in 2024 to help give his team more financial flexibility to build a strong squad, and two years later, the Knicks won their first NBA championship in 53 seasons.

In the latest edition of Boardroom Talks, Houston Rockets forward Kevin Durant was asked by Speedy Morman if he would make a similar move (8:20 mark). He provided the following response.

Offseason Overreactions for Every Team 🫨

"I mean, I don't think I would be advised to do that. I mean, I would have got talked out of it. I probably would have been like, 'All right, I'm cool with it.' And then I'd have sat down and talked to all my people like I usually do, [Rich Kleiman], all my friends, everyone would have been like, 'What are you serious? Why do you need to take that risk when this dude's a billionaire?'

"You know what I'm saying? But I understand his thought process and why he actually executed that. I can't put myself in that position and just say, yeah, I would have did it or not. But for him to make that decision and then come out the way it did, kudos to him, but hopefully he gets that back at the back end."

Brunson signed a four-year, $156.5 milllion max deal in 2024. If he waited one year, Brunson would have been eligible for a five-year, $269 million deal in 2025.

Adrian Wojnarowski, then of ESPN, broke it all down.

The Knicks made important moves in 2024 to build their roster.

One month before the Brunson deal, New York signed OG Anunoby to a five-year, $212.5 million contract .

Soon after the Brunson move, the Knicks traded for Brooklyn Nets wing Mikal Bridges. They signed him to a four-year, $150 million extension one year later. The Knicks also added Minnesota Timberwolves center Karl-Anthony Towns via trade in Oct. 2024.

Brunson certainly made an unprecedented financial sacrifice for the good of the team. It's certainly understandable if other players (or those players' representatives) wouldn't be in favor of such moves. However, it worked out quite well for the Knicks.

articles.title: Kevin Durant Reveals Best 'On Paper' Team He's Played for Between Warriors, Nets in New Video
articles.summary: Kevin Durant says the best on-paper roster he's ever been a part of didn't belong to the mid-dynasty Golden State Warriors.
articles.body:
Kevin Durant says the best on-paper roster he's ever been a part of didn't belong to the mid-dynasty Golden State Warriors.

"Just looking at straight roster, nothing else—yeah, I would say Brooklyn," Durant said when asked about the best team of his career on a Thursday episode of Boardroom Talks .

Durant joined the Nets ahead of the 2019-20 season. Players including Kyrie Irving, James Harden, Blake Griffin, LaMarcus Aldridge, Patty Mills and Paul Millsap played for the franchise during his tenure in Brooklyn, culminating with a dramatic seven-game series against the Milwaukee Bucks in the 2021 playoffs.

Durant had in 2016 joined a Warriors team that won 73 games the season prior thanks to a roster led by Klay Thompson, Stephen Curry and Draymond Green.

"We had the names on that team, when just looking at straight paper," Durant said. "I know people want to say, 'The Warriors had Steph and Klay.' But I'm like, when you look at that team— at the time, Steph was an MVP, but Klay and Draymond din't get the accolades at that time."

"These dudes I'm talking about already completed their careers, damn near, and on top of me, James and Kyrie... when you're just putting accolades on the table, I would say that [Nets] team."

This isn't the first time Durant has referred to a lack of accolades earned by Warriors players at the time he joined the franchise.

He wrote on social media earlier this summer the 2026-27 Philadelphia 76ers were stronger than the dynasty Warriors on paper in part because Thompson was "never a MVP candidate in nothing."

Regardless of individual honors, Durant told Boardroom the Warriors' 2018 or 2019 teams were the best of his 18-year NBA career.

Durant is heading into his 19th NBA campaign and his second year with the Rockets after averaging 26 points per game last season.

The Rockets are hoping to win a playoff series for the first time since 2020 next spring after bolstering their own roster with the offseason additions of Bogdan Bogdanović and Marcus Smart.

articles.title: Kevin Durant and LeBron James Recorded 3 Rap Songs Together, Rockets Star Reveals in New Video
articles.summary: Kevin Durant and LeBron James apparently recorded more songs together than the single track that was released in 2018.
articles.body:
Kevin Durant and LeBron James apparently recorded more songs together than the single track that was released in 2018.

The duo recorded multiple tracks while working out in Akron around 2011, Durant told Boardroom's Speedy Morman around the 50:00 mark of Thursday's Boardroom Talks podcast.

"We had like three songs, I think... Me and Rich Paul really were the ones that got it going and convinced Bron to rap," Durant told Morman.

Durant continued, "Any time somebody does something for the first few times, it's forced, a little forced. Once you get that flow— he had to figure it out. He loved rap."

When asked where the songs were now, Durant said, "That's a good question. They're in that studio in Akron. Somebody out there, engineer somebody, got them."

Producer Franky Wahoo released in 2018 a track called "It Ain't Easy" that featured James and Durant rapping.

The track was recorded during the 2011 NBA lockout while Durant was signed with the Oklahoma City Thunder and James was a member of the Miami Heat, according to ESPN .

Durant told Morman the song that was released featured a different beat than the one he and James had initially rapped over.

"They changed the beat, and it just made the song even more wack," Durant said.

Should other tracks featuring Durant and James surface, they could be worth a significant amount of money. Wahoo said TMZ originally tried to purchase "It Ain't Easy" for $250,000 in 2017.

articles.title: Riley Gaines endorses Ken Paxton for Senate, cites fight to protect women's sports
articles.summary: Riley Gaines endorsed Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, citing his NCAA lawsuit and contrasting his record with James Talarico on transgender athletes.
articles.body: Women’s sports advocate Riley Gaines endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in his U.S. Senate race against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, pointing to the candidates’ sharply different records on transgender athletes and medical treatments for minors. "Texas needs a senator who will fight without apology for women, for kids, and for the health of every American family," Gaines said in a statement. "Ken Paxton is that leader, and I am proud to support and endorse him." Gaines, a former University of Kentucky swimmer, became a prominent advocate for preserving female-only athletic divisions after tying transgender swimmer Lia Thomas in the 200-yard freestyle at the 2022 NCAA championships. TEXAS AG KEN PAXTON SENDS MESSAGE TO WNBA AMID 'CONCERNS' OVER TREATMENT OF SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SUPPORTERS She praised Paxton as a "relentless fighter for the protection of children" and highlighted his legal action against the NCAA. "He has taken decisive action against those who would expose our children to irreversible harm and refused to be silent while the radical left was putting the next generation in danger," Gaines said. "He even filed a major lawsuit against the NCAA to keep men out of women’s sports." Paxton sued the NCAA in December 2024, accusing the organization of violating the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act by marketing competitions as women’s events while allowing transgender athletes to participate. The lawsuit sought to prevent transgender athletes from competing in NCAA women’s events involving Texas teams or taking place in the state. The NCAA later changed its policy in February 2025 to restrict women’s competition to athletes who were female at birth. Paxton has also filed lawsuits against doctors he accused of violating a Texas law prohibiting certain transition-related treatments for minors. TALARICO'S MOVE TO SWAP OUT 'WOMAN' RESURFACES AMID BACKLASH OVER SIMILAR BILL IN NY: 'INSANE INDIVIDUAL' Gaines contrasted Paxton’s record with that of Talarico, who opposed legislation requiring Texas public-school athletes to compete on teams corresponding with their biological sex. "His opponent, James Talarico, is a far-left extremist who has refused to accept biological reality," Gaines said. "He has repeatedly put women’s safety, privacy, and opportunities in danger by championing a radical agenda that forces biological males into girls’ and women’s sports, locker rooms, and private spaces." During debate over a school sports bill in 2021, Talarico argued that biological sex could be "a spectrum" and invoked his Christian faith while defending transgender children. He later said he still believes transgender people deserve "dignity and equality," although he would express some of his earlier comments differently today. The Texas Tribune reported that Talarico opposed the legislation that ultimately became Texas’ school sports law. Talarico has separately said he opposes gender-reassignment surgery for minors. His campaign has argued that Republican attacks distort his position and ignore his objections to the broader scope of Texas’ treatment restrictions. PolitiFact reported in June that advertisements depicting Talarico as supporting such surgeries were inaccurate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Paxton defeated longtime Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican runoff in May. Talarico defeated Rep. Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary. The two will face each other in the Nov. 3 general election, which has emerged as one of the country’s most competitive Senate contests.

articles.title: Great Britain: Tosan Evbuomwan impresses as GB cruise past Switzerland in EuroBasket pre-qualifier
articles.summary: Great Britain start their pre-qualifying campaign for the 2029 EuroBasket tournament with a convincing win over Switzerland.
articles.body:
Great Britain started their pre-qualifying campaign for 2029 EuroBasket with a convincing 110-75 win over Switzerland in Fribourg.

Boston Celtics centre Amari Williams and Barcelona forward Tosan Evbuomwan both made their debuts for Great Britain's senior side in the victory to put GB top of Group E.

Evbuomwan, who spent three years in the NBA, making 50 appearances prior to his move to Barcelona earlier this summer, contributed 21points in 25 minutes.

His added NBA quality alongside Williams , who has just finished his first season with the Celtics, allowed GB to claim an impressive win.

Williams posted eight points and seven rebounds in 19 minutes, while Josh Uduje top scored with 24 points for the visitors.

Marc Steutel's side were comfortable from the off in their first competitive match since missing out on qualifying for the 2027 Fiba World Cup.

Great Britain won each of the four quarters, taking the opening two by six points each.

Ranked 45th in the world with their opponents 16 places below them, Great Britain cemented their dominance after half-time to lead 79-51 at the end of the third quarter.

With one eye on Sunday's match against Slovakia in Newcastle, Evbuomwan and Williams were among those afforded some rest time in the fourth quarter.

Their remaining two fixtures are a home match against Switzerland on November 29, before travelling to Slovakia on February 25, 2027.

The winner of each pre-qualifying group will reach full qualifying, taking place in 2028 and 2029. Should Great Britain finish not finish top, they will enter a third round of pre-qualifying in 2027.

articles.title: Michael Jordan's 41st Signature Shoe Revealed in New Photos From Jordan Brand
articles.summary: Jordan Brand has revealed the newest addition to Michael Jordan's signature shoe collection.
articles.body:
Jordan Brand has revealed the newest addition to Michael Jordan's signature shoe collection.

The sneaker company unveiled the Jordan 41 on Thursday, featuring photos of the legendary Chicago Bull with his new shoe.

According to a release from Jordan Brand, the Jordan 41 "marks an evolution of Jordan Brand heritage style, embracing a future-forward approach that pushes the boundaries of innovation and expression."

The shoe will have a limited release in China on Friday, with a global release to come at a later date.

Jordan's first signature shoe was released in 1985, and his sneakers have since gone on to be a basketball and cultural staple.

A number of NBA stars wore the Jordan 40, including the Orlando Magic's Paolo Banchero and the Washington Wizards' Trae Young. That will likely be the case for the Jordan 41 as well, as one of the greatest players in NBA history continues to put out iconic shoes.

articles.title: Heat Reportedly Sign Nick Richards After Klay Thompson Contract, Updated Depth Chart
articles.summary: After bringing in Klay Thompson last week, the Miami Heat have added some frontcourt depth ahead of the 2026-27 campaign.
articles.body:
After bringing in Klay Thompson last week, the Miami Heat have added some frontcourt depth ahead of the 2026-27 campaign.

Per ESPN's Shams Charania, the Heat have signed center Nick Richards to a one-year deal.

Richards, a second-round pick in 2020, spent the first four years of his career with the Charlotte Hornets before being traded to the Phoenix Suns during the 2024-25 campaign.

The Chicago Bulls traded for Richards in February ahead of the trade deadline.

He's coming off a season in which he posted 5.8 points and 5.1 boards per game across 48 contests. It was a relatively down year for him as he played just 14.6 minutes per contest.

The Heat have been eyeing roster upgrades since making a blockbuster trade for Giannis Antetokounmpo earlier this summer, but they haven't exactly had the means to make any major signings.

Richards isn't a premier signing, but he at least gives Miami some much needed depth in the frontcourt, and joining the team on a veteran minimum means the Heat will stay below the first apron.

The deal comes after Miami signed the sharpshooting veteran Thompson to a two-year, $11.5 million contract following a buyout with the Dallas Mavericks. Shooting was a main priority for the Heat heading into the season, and they managed to pick up one of the best three-point specialists in NBA history.

Whether the two new roster additions will give Miami enough to compete in a loaded Eastern Conference remains to be seen.
